title: About
text:
This project aims to provide a look at the data behind active travel decisions in Scotland.
In 2020 The Scottish Government set a target to reduce car kilometres by 20%, which in part has shaped the active travel framework guiding transport policy. That target is currently not on track, and this blog looks at the numbers behind where implementation is working — and where it needs more support.

title: About
text:
Who runs The Mode Shift?
I’m Steve Crawford, based in Inverness. I’m a strong believer in the transformative power of bikes on people and communities. I have equal love for cycling as a sport and cycling as a mode of transport.
One of the most constant thoughts in my head is ‘what does that number mean?’, so I recently put my money where my mouth is and completed an MSc in Data Analytics at University of Highlands and Islands. This project is a way for me to merge those two passions while hopefully helping improve Active Travel decision making in Scotland.

title: About
text:
Methodology
Wherever possible the analysis in this blog is carried out using open source tools. Most code is written in R using the Tidyverse set of packages and datasets used are publicly available.

title: Millburn Road - Cycling Volume Analysis
text: This is the third in a series of posts about a cycle lane in Millburn Road, Inverness. The previous post, detailing where we’re getting the data from can be found here.

title: Millburn Road - Cycling Volume Analysis
section: What data are we looking at?
text:
What data are we looking at?
I’ve decided to concentrate on the main entry points and routes through the city. There’s a continuous counter placed anywhere you see this icon  on the map below1:



Image taken from Cycling Scotland Open Data portal (usmart.io)


This gives counts at the following locations:



Millburn Road
Ness Walk
Greig Street



Huntly Street
Academy Street
Crown Road



Bank Street
Bridge Street
Castle Road



Both Millburn Road and Academy Street have two counters each, one for eastbound and one for westbound traffic. Since this analysis isn’t interested in the directional distinction, they have been combined into one count for each street.

title: Millburn Road - Cycling Volume Analysis
text:
Cycling volume history
The first number we want to look at is just how busy each counter is with cycle traffic. Figure 1 shows all of the cycle traffic volume data since collection started in March 2021. Millburn Road is highlighted orange, and you can mouse over the other lines to see which counter they correspond to.








Figure 1: Average daily cycle counts by road, 2021–2026




A couple of things stand out on the chart before we address Millburn Road. The first is that the data in the 2021-2022 period looks quite messy. I think it’s reasonable to say that the travel patterns in the early post-pandemic years is sufficiently different to where we are now to give that data a separate look another time.
The second thing is the steep drop in counts at all sites in the winter 2024/25 period. I don’t know enough yet to explain it, but I do want to say I’m working on figuring it out and will publish what I find. It’s worth noting that cycle traffic appears to be overall lower after this blip. Until I know more about whether that’s real or an artefact of data collection, I’ll refrain from commenting on any trends over time.
Figure 2 shows the data starting in January 2023:








Figure 2: Average daily cycle counts by road, 2023–2026




It’s clear that the Millburn Road counter has consistently been among the highest counts in the city. Other sites with similarly high cycling volume are Huntly Street (coloured ochre) and Ness Walk (coloured blue). The significant dip in volume in 2023/24 on Ness Walk was caused by its closure to upgrade the cycling infrastructure there (yay!).
Since 2025 is the most recent full year for which we have data2, the median count at each site in that year also gives a useful picture.

title: Millburn Road - Cycling Volume Analysis
text:
The Mode Shift Share
A really important measure when looking at any mode of transport is its share of the overall traffic in the data. Mode share (sometimes called modal share) is the kind of measure you could name a blog after.
Figure 3 and Table 2 show the mode share companions to our volume data:








Figure 3: Cycling mode share by road, 2023–2026

You may have had the same initial gut instinct as me - yikes. Millburn Road plummets down the table to nestle between Castle Road and Bank Street, neither of which is a big hitter in the cycle volume league above. Millburn’s previous contenders, Ness Walk and Huntly street stay at the top of the charts, with their mode share towering above all others.
However, if we take the raw volume into account as well as the mode share it actually highlights Millburn Road as being uniquely good at getting bikes through. Ness Walk and Huntly Street have high cycle volumes and high mode shares in part because relative to the other sites they have low numbers of motor vehicles. Millburn Road carries a similar volume of cyclists but with much more motor traffic. This is really clear to see if we look at the motor vehicle counts as well:

title: Millburn Road - Cycling Volume Analysis
text:
Conclusion
It’s fairly clear that historically, Millburn Road is unique within Inverness city centre for its ability to transport large numbers of cyclists alongside heavy motor traffic. This in itself is not entirely surprising as it contained the only section of segregated cycle lane next to a busy road in the city but it does highlight the importance of that lane.
To me, this makes the Highland Council’s decision to remove a section of it right at the most complex junction seem to go against their stated vision to make active travel an attractive and realistic choice for more people, more often, for more of their everyday journeys. I hope they will take a good look at this data as they plan for how they will move forward at that site. I think it makes a good case for improving and indeed extending the cycle lane along that corridor to enable even more people to arrive in the city by bicycle.

title: Millburn Road, Inverness - The Background
text:
To open this project I’m going to have a look at some infrastructure that is close to home - the segregated bike lane on Millburn Road in Inverness.
During the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, cities across Scotland installed lots of temporary bike lanes as people’s travel habits changes in response to the virus. One such lane was built along a stretch of Millburn Road1 protecting cyclists on a particularly busy route into the city. The road went from looking like this in 2017:
To this in 2025:
So you can see it’s gone from a fairly inhospitable place to cycle, to one that’s fairly attractive. Then in a surprising move earlier this year Highland Council removed a section at the westernmost junction.
Over the next few weeks I’m going to explore some of the data around this junction to investigate how useful it’s been to the city. I want to see what we can learn from the infrastructure to help better inform any plans for what comes next.

title: Inverness Courier - Bad 20mph Stats
text:
This article in the Inverness Courier was brought to my attention and it immediately brought up some statistical red flags. Road safety is an important factor in active travel and I feel it’s important to challenge bad stats when we see them. I’ve written directly to the Courier as well as the MSP quoted in the article, Tim Eagle, with some of my objections but I’d like to go into more detail here.
The article suggests that the Scottish Governments expansion of 20mph speed limits on its road networks is not successful because of a slight rise in road traffic collisions in 20mph zones in 2025. Here I’m going to list my red flags and explain in detail why this article should not be taken seriously.

title: Inverness Courier - Bad 20mph Stats
section: A Better Use of the Data
text:
A Better Use of the Data
I don’t want to just sit here and criticise the article, I want to see if there’s something we can genuinely learn from the data if we treat it with more respect. I’ll add links to my primary data throughout.

✅ A Better Denominator
As I mention above, a more meaningful statistic is possible here if we put the collisions in the correct context. I’ve tried to find a breakdown of the length of each road in Scotland by speed limit but the closest thing I can find is in Transport Scotland’s Scottish Transport Statistics 2025 Report. Near the bottom of that page is the link to the Excel sheets for Chapter 4 - Road Network, where the roads are broken down into ‘Roads up to 40mph’ and ‘Roads over 40mph’. This isn’t granular enough for looking at specific speed limits, so I’ve sent an FOI to Transport Scotland to see if they hold the data at individual speed limit level.
The same report details traffic volumes in Chapter 5 - Road Traffic. The published dataset splits the traffic volume estimates (given in million vehicle kilometers) by road type rather than speed limit. The distinction of minor/major roads doesn’t map perfectly with speed limits - some minor roads will have high speed limits and vice versa - but the vast majority of roads affected by the 20mph roll-out will be minor roads. Here, I’m having to make a judgement call about the compromise I have to make in the data, but crucially I’ve also stated my defense for my choice. I’ll proceed with this with the caveat that it contains volumes of traffic on roads that we’re not interested in. Here’s the trend in that measure from the data:








Figure 5: Traffic volume on minor roads (B, C and unclassified) in Scotland, 2021–2024






✅ A Defensible Subset of Data
Time to focus on which data will tell us something useful. Given the focus of the question is whether the 20mph policy improves road safety, I think it’s important to consider the desired outcome of the policy. The Scottish Goverment’s Implementation for 20mph limits highlights the importance of reducing the severity of collisions:

The speed of a vehicle directly influences the risk of a collision as well as the severity of injuries sustained, and the likelihood of death resulting from that collision.

With that in mind, choosing to focus on collisions in which one or more casualty is killed or seriously injured (so-called KSI collisions) allows both the frequency and severity of collisions to be covered in the analysis. Again, this is a choice that I have made to exclude some data from my analysis but I’ve made clear my reason for doing so. Here’s that trend, not corrected for traffic volume:








Figure 6: KSI collisions on minor roads (B, C and unclassified) in Scotland, 2021–2024






✅ A Realistic Conclusion
You may have noticed that I don’t have any data for 2025 above - that’s because I don’t have the traffic volume data for 2025 yet. This limits the scope of the conclusions we can make but it doesn’t mean we can’t learn something. Here’s the KSI collision rate corrected for traffic volume:








Figure 7: KSI collisions per billion vehicle-km on minor roads in Scotland, 2021–2024




There’s no clear trend on display here, but we can see that 2023 and 2024 have higher traffic-adjusted rates of KSI collisions than the preceding years. There’s nothing in this data that point to a cause for that rise but it’s there and it’s real. Here’s my attempt at a statistically defensible headline from that data:






Serious crash rate on minor roads averaged 7.5% higher in 2023–24 than 2021–22.



And that’s it. There’s no evidence that 20mph zones may have caused it, no evidence of a war on motorists. Just and indication of something that could be a problem - the kind of problem that needs an intervention to fix it.

title: Inverness Courier - Bad 20mph Stats
text:
Footnotes


My own pull of the same STATS19 data gives 522 collisions in 2021 and 482 in 2023, not 515 and 488 as quoted here. STATS19 records are periodically revised as late reports and corrections come in, so this is most likely a difference in when each of us pulled the data, rather than an error on either side.↩︎

title: Millburn Road - The Data
text:
To understand more about the bike lane on Millburn Road, I wanted to look at the cycling traffic levels right across the city of Inverness. The excellent news is that Cycling Scotland have an Open Data portal that tracks lots of places across Scotland. The less great news is that the data starts in 2021, so there’s no simple before/after picture to see the effect of the installation of new bike lanes during the COVID-19 pandemic. There’s still a lot to learn from what is there though!
Millburn Road has two traffic counters, one each for the Eastward and Westward sections of the road. The point where the counters appear on the map is almost exactly where the section of bike lane has been removed making it a good place to measure bike traffic:



Image taken from Cycling Scotland Open Data portal (usmart.io)


By grabbing the data from both the Eastward and Westward counters it’s pretty easy to see which side of the road has a bike lane:








Figure 1: Average daily cycle counts on Millburn Road by direction, 2022–2026




After a look to see if the data is what we want (it is) we can then download the full dataset for the Highland Council area. This gives daily aggregated counts at each site of cyclists, pedestrians, motorcycles, cars, buses, and goods vehicles from March 2021 to June 2026.
In the next post, we’ll look at how the cycle counts compare to the other city centre sites:



Image taken from Cycling Scotland Open Data portal (usmart.io)
